PASSO 1: o discurso directo reproduz as: STEP 1: direct speech gives someone's exact words, in quotation marks or with a dash: Ana dijo: «Trabajo en Madrid». Reported speech tells what she said, without quotation marks: «Ana dijo que trabajaba en Madrid» (Ana said she worked in Madrid). STEP 2: «que» joins the verb of saying to the reported sentence. English can drop "that" ("she said she worked…"); Spanish never drops «que». STEP 3: if the verb of saying is in the present or the pretérito perfecto («dice que», «ha dicho que»), the reported verb doesn't change: «Ana dice que trabaja en Madrid». STEP 4: if the verb of saying is in the past («dijo que», «me contó que», «preguntó»), the tenses shift back — exactly like English backshift: present → imperfecto ("works" → "worked"); pretérito perfecto and indefinido → pluscuamperfecto ("has finished" / "finished" → "had finished"); future → conditional ("will" → "would"); imperative → imperfecto de subjuntivo. STEP 5: the imperfecto, the pluscuamperfecto and the conditional don't change: «Vivía en Lima» stays «vivía». STEP 6: if the fact is still true, or the speaker wants to stress it, the original tense can stay: «Dijo que Madrid es la capital». But when in doubt, shift back. STEP 7: a present subjunctive shifts to the imperfecto de subjuntivo: «Quiero que vengas» becomes «Dijo que quería que viniera». STEP 8: more precise verbs than «decir» introduce reported speech: «contar, explicar, comentar, responder, añadir, avisar, afirmar, negar». Use them for variety.

The differences: «que» can never be dropped, and question words keep their accent in reported questions («dónde», «qué»).

PASSO 1: no discurso directo, palavras c: STEP 1: in direct speech, words like «hoy», «aquí», «este» depend on when and where the person is speaking. When you report the sentence later or elsewhere, these words must change — as in English ("today" → "that day"). STEP 2: time markers change like this: «hoy» → «ese día» (that day); «ayer» → «el día anterior» or «la víspera» (the day before); «mañana» → «al día siguiente» (the next day); «ahora» → «entonces» (then); «hace dos días» → «dos días antes» (two days before); «la semana que viene» → «la semana siguiente»; «el año pasado» → «el año anterior». STEP 3: place markers and demonstratives change: «aquí» → «allí» or «allá» (there); «este» → «ese» or «aquel»; «ven» (come here) → «fuera» (go there), as in «me dijo que fuera». STEP 4: pronouns change person: «Mi casa es grande», said by Ana, becomes «Ana dijo que su casa era grande». «Te llamaré», said to you, becomes «me dijo que me llamaría». STEP 5: point of view matters. If you're reporting on the same day or in the same place, you don't need to change: if Ana told you in the morning «Hoy salgo temprano» and you report it that evening, you can say «Ana dijo que hoy salía temprano». STEP 6: «ir» and «venir» also adapt to where the speaker is. «Ven a mi casa» can be reported as «Me dijo que fuera a su casa» or, if you're there, «Me dijo que viniera a su casa». STEP 7: in writing, when the sentence has more than one verb, shift all of them: «Dijo que había llegado la víspera y que se iría al día siguiente».

PASSO 1: pergunta de sim ou não vira ind: STEP 1: English "ask" is two Spanish verbs. Asking a QUESTION is «preguntar»; asking FOR something or asking someone TO DO something is «pedir». A yes/no question becomes «si» (if / whether): «¿Vienes?» → «Me preguntó si venía» (She asked if I was coming). No «que» before it: «preguntó si», not «preguntó que si». STEP 2: a question with a question word keeps it, with its accent, but without «¿ ?»: «¿Dónde vives?» → «Me preguntó dónde vivía» (She asked where I lived). «¿Qué quieres?» → «Me preguntó qué quería». STEP 3: the verb of the question follows the same tense changes as in session 1. STEP 4: requests and commands become «que» + imperfecto de subjuntivo. English uses an infinitive here — "She told me TO SIT down", "He asked me NOT TO TALK" — Spanish can't: «Siéntate» → «Me pidió que me sentara»; «No hables» → «Me pidió que no hablara». STEP 5: see the difference between informing and ordering: «Me dijo que venía» (He told me he was coming — information) and «Me dijo que viniera» (He told me to come — an order). The mood tells them apart. STEP 6: with «invitar», use «a» + infinitive or «a que» + subjunctive: «Me invitó a cenar», «Me invitó a que cenara con ella». STEP 7: in indirect questions with a question word, the subject usually goes after the verb: «Preguntó cuándo llegaba el tren» (She asked when the train was arriving).

And English "She told me TO COME" uses an infinitive; Spanish needs «que» + subjunctive: «Me dijo que viniera». Compare «Me dijo que venía» (He told me he was coming).
